candidates.label: Gethsemane
candidates.support: Wikidata's coordinate for the traditional garden is corroborated by OpenBible.info's independently recorded point for the same site, at the foot of the Mount of Olives across the Kidron Valley from the Temple Mount. The general area is not disputed, but the exact garden plot is: at least two distinct denominational traditions claim the site, about 200 meters apart, including a Franciscan-custodied garden by the Church of All Nations and a Russian Orthodox garden near the Church of Mary Magdalene, and no first-century boundary of 'the garden' itself is archaeologically fixed.

summary.text: Gethsemane is a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem's Temple Mount and a short walk from the city. Its name comes from an Aramaic or Hebrew phrase, gat shemanim, for an olive-oil press, which fits its traditional identification as an olive grove. Olive trees have grown on the mount's slopes for thousands of years, and in Jewish tradition it was also called the "Mount of Unction," because oil from its olives was used to anoint the king and the high priest.

history.text: According to Matthew and Mark, Jesus came to Gethsemane with his disciples on the night of his arrest and told them to sit while he prayed. Mark says he came back and found them sleeping, went away to pray again, returned to find them asleep a second time, and came back a third time. John, without naming the place, says Jesus and his disciples crossed the brook Kidron into "a garden," and that Judas came there with a detachment of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, carrying lanterns, torches and weapons.

Today several churches mark places at the foot of the Mount of Olives linked to that night. The best-known garden, beside the Basilica of the Agony (the Church of All Nations), has been owned by the Franciscans since 1681 and holds eight of the oldest olive trees in the world. A study released in 2012 dated wood from three of them to 1092, 1166 and 1198, and DNA tests found that the trees were planted from the same parent plant. Because olive trees can grow back from their roots, the researchers said this does not settle whether they go back to Jesus' time.

scripture.textWEB: Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go there and pray.”
They came to a place which was named Gethsemane. He said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”

He came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “Simon, are you sleeping? Couldn’t you watch one hour? Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. Again he returned and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy; and they didn’t know what to answer him. He came the third time and said to them, “Sleep on now, and take your rest. It is enough. The hour has come. Behold, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.
When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.
Judas then, having taken a detachment of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons.

politicalHistory.note: Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch."

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Quirinius, governing Syria, conducted a census at the start of this period. Luke 2:1-2 is dated by some instead to the time of Herod's birth narrative, before 4 BC, rather than to Quirinius's AD 6 census; this note does not resolve the question.
